newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Argentine minister "beginning to like" Falklanders.
newsitem.headline: Argentine minister "beginning to like" Falklanders.

text.p: Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella said on Monday he was committed to the well being of Falkland Islanders and was "beginning to like them," even though they were in the wrong.
He was addressing the U.N. decolonization committee on the question of the Falklands, the British south Atlantic colony claimed by Argentina, which calls them Las Malvinas.
Britain and Argentina went to war in 1982 over the islands after they were occupied briefly by Argentine troops.

Delivering part of his speech in English instead of Spanish, "as a token of deference for and respect for the islanders," Di Tella said: "We are friends of them. We are not their enemies. We are not threatening them."
Although the controversy was between Argentina and Britain, he said he was very conscious that the British parliament would not disregard the islanders' views.
"In this connection I want to express that we also care -- we care about them and we are committed to their well being."

Departing from the prepared text of his remarks in English, Di Tella continued: "I'm going to say something more. I have been meeting islanders from time to time -- not as often as I would want -- and although this may be undiplomatic, I am beginning to like them. I like the strength with which they put their case. They are wrong, but I like them," he added, referring to their wish to remain British.

"The worst thing I can do is to win an argument. I want to win their hearts. It will be much more difficult ... I am sure that if we get together, we will be able to reach agreements which would surprise both of us now."
Di Tella stressed that, although Argentina had a territorial claim, "we have committed ourselves through our constitution to recover the islands exclusively by peaceful means."

Britain, which is not a member of the U.N. decolonization committee, has resumed relations and cooperation with Argentina on a range of topics since the Falklands war but refuses to discuss the issue of sovereignty.

Speaking in Spanish, Di Tella noted he was addressing the committee for the first time since the installation of a new secretary-general, Kofi Annan, and of a "new government in the United Kingdom, with a clear majority in parliament, with which we expect to continue the dialogue initiated with the previous government."
Di Tella told reporters he would meet British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook in London on July 23.

In his speech to the committee, Di Tella said that, in cases of contested sovereignty, the territorial dispute must be resolved first, and only at a later stage should the applicability of the principle of self-determination be analysed. To back this argument, he quoted from a recent book by the British member of the World Court, Judge Rosalyn Higgins.

Di Tella also quoted from a 1967 U.N. General Assembly resolution that said any colonial situation that partially or completed destroyed the national unity and territorial integrity of a country was incompatible with the purposes and principles of the U.N. Charter.

"The restitution of Hong Kong on July 1 of this year and of Macau in 1999 to the People's Republic of China is the most recent proof of the unchangeable validity of the territorial integrity principle," he said.

"Furthermore, this demonstrates that administering powers, under certain circumstances, can indeed change their opinion through dialogue and negotiation. This shows no weakness, only indeed shows their maturity."
